name: Challenger’s top half
intro: This is where the top half of Challenger crashed on 15 December 1972, about 10 km from the landing site. It had carried Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt off the Moon the day before, the last launch from the Moon so far. Its crater has not been found.

hotspots.title: The last liftoff
hotspots.text: On 14 December 1972 this cabin blasted off from Taurus-Littrow while the rover’s camera, steered from Houston, followed it into the sky.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 17 return to orbit

photo.alt: A blurry TV picture of a spacecraft rising above grey mountains with sparks below it.
photo.caption: Challenger’s cabin lifts off, seen on TV from the parked rover.

hotspots.title: Somewhere here
hotspots.text: The cabin hit about 10 km southwest of the landing site. Its crater has never been identified.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Nearly sideways
hotspots.text: It came in only 4.9 degrees above the horizon, so it probably skidded and broke up rather than digging one round crater.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: The valley listened
hotspots.text: The geophones the crew had left at the science station felt the crash, helping map the layers under the valley.

funFact: It hit the Moon at about 1.67 km per second, almost sideways, just 4.9 degrees above the horizon.
whyLeft: After the last moonwalkers moved into the command module America, the cabin had no way home, so it was crashed near the valley to shake the instruments the crew had left.
repurpose: Only fragments remain, somewhere near Taurus-Littrow. Finding them would show how spacecraft break up in a sideways crash.

source.label: Estimate; never located (NSSDCA: impact point from tracking only)
